title: Tell me about a time you made a fast decision with incomplete information
prompt: Tell me about a time you had to make an important decision quickly, without all the information you'd have liked. What was the situation, how did you decide, and what happened?
blurb: Bias for action: did they move decisively on limited info AND manage the risk — or just gamble?

rubric.label: Situation & time pressure
rubric.description: Sets up a real decision under time pressure with genuine uncertainty and stakes — clear on what info was missing and why waiting was costly.

rubric.label: Owning the call
rubric.description: Shows THEY made the decision (or drove it) rather than deferring, and understood why speed mattered more than certainty here.

rubric.label: Decision process & risk management
rubric.description: Describes how they decided fast without being reckless — the data they did gather, the assumptions made, and how they made the move reversible or bounded the downside.

rubric.label: Result & impact
rubric.description: States the outcome and quantifies the value of moving fast (or the cost avoided), honestly including if it went partly wrong.

rubric.label: Reflection & calibration
rubric.description: Shows judgment about when to move fast vs when to gather more — the reversibility test — and what they learned about calibrating speed vs certainty.

rubric.label: Communication & structure
rubric.description: Structured, concise, and clear about the reasoning at the moment of decision.

reference.scenario: The candidate should recall a decision where waiting for full information was itself costly — a production incident, a fast-closing market or partnership window, a customer ultimatum, a launch go/no-go — and they moved decisively on partial data. The best answers show calibrated risk-taking: they distinguished a reversible from an irreversible decision and bounded the downside, rather than gambling.
model_points: Situation: a concrete moment with a closing window, where the cost of delay was real and full certainty was impossible.
Task: they took responsibility for making the call rather than escalating endlessly or waiting for perfect data.
Action: gathered the highest-value information quickly, made explicit assumptions, and chose — often framing it as a reversible/two-way-door decision so speed was safe.
Action: bounded the downside — a rollback plan, a canary, a small bet, a checkpoint — and communicated the decision and its assumptions to stakeholders.
Result: quantified the payoff of moving fast (incident contained, window captured, weeks saved) or, if it went wrong, how the reversibility they built in limited the damage.
Reflection: articulates a mental model for when to move fast vs when the decision is one-way and warrants more diligence; how they calibrated after this.

probes.trigger: decision sounds reckless / no risk mitigation
probes.question: What was your downside if you were wrong, and what did you do to limit it? Was this reversible?

probes.trigger: claims they had no information at all
probes.question: You had some signal — what did you gather in the time you had, and what did you decide to stop waiting for?
What would waiting have cost? How do you know moving fast was worth it?
It worked out — but was it a good decision, or a lucky one? How would you know the difference?
When would you deliberately slow down and gather more before deciding? How do you tell the two apart?

red_flags: Reckless gamble with no attempt to bound the downside or gather cheap signal.
Confuses bias for action with impulsiveness — no reasoning, just 'I went with my gut'.
Actually escalated or waited and is dressing it up as decisiveness.
No sense of reversibility — treats a one-way-door decision the same as a two-way one.
Judges the decision purely by outcome; can't separate a good decision from a lucky result.
No reflection on calibration; 'move fast always' with no awareness of when it backfires.
follow_ups: How do you decide which decisions are safe to make fast and which need more diligence?
Tell me about a time moving fast backfired. What did you take from it?
How did you bring stakeholders along when you couldn't fully justify the call yet?
What information would have changed your decision, and was it worth the wait to get it?
reference.exemplar_answer: Situation: 'During a Friday deploy, error rates on our payment API started climbing — not a full outage, but a steady rise in failed charges. The obvious suspect was the release we'd just shipped, but confirming it would take an hour of log analysis, and every minute meant lost transactions.' Task: 'I was on call and had to decide: keep digging to be sure, or roll back now on a strong-but-unconfirmed hypothesis.' Action: 'I checked the two cheapest signals — the timing lined up exactly with the deploy, and the errors clustered in the changed code path. That was enough. I rolled back immediately, because a rollback was a two-way door: if I was wrong, we'd lose ten minutes and could re-deploy. I posted my assumption in the incident channel so others could challenge it, then did the full root-cause after we'd stopped the bleeding.' Result: 'Error rates normalized within five minutes; we contained roughly $X of failed transactions versus the hour a careful investigation would have cost. Root cause confirmed it was the release.' Reflection: 'The key was recognizing this was reversible — that let me move on partial evidence safely. For a one-way decision I'd have spent the hour. I've since made 'is this a one-way or two-way door?' the first question I ask under time pressure.'

interviewer_notes: The core signal is calibrated risk-taking, not raw speed. Probe the downside and whether they made the move reversible — this separates bias for action from recklessness. Watch for the opposite failure too: candidates who dressed up waiting/escalating as decisiveness. Always run the 'good decision vs lucky outcome' probe — strong candidates can defend the decision on the information they had at the time, independent of how it turned out. Reflection should reveal a model for one-way vs two-way doors. Push for a quantified cost-of-delay.
